text: So Abram went up from Egypt to the Negev, he and his wife and all he owned, and Lot with him.
Abram had grown very wealthy in livestock, in silver, and in gold.
He journeyed on by stages from the Negev as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had stood at the first, between Bethel and Ai—

versions.text: He journeyed on by stages from the Negev toward Bethel, to the place where his tent had stood at the first, between Bethel and Ai—
versions.explanation: The Hebrew וְעַד marks the endpoint reached ('as far as'), not merely the direction of travel ('toward'). Abram actually arrived at the site, as verse 4 confirms.

text: to the place of the altar he had built there earlier. And there Abram called on the name of the LORD.
Lot, who traveled with Abram, also had flocks and herds and tents,
and the land could not support them living side by side. Their possessions were so great that they could not stay together.
So quarreling broke out between Abram's herdsmen and Lot's herdsmen. At that time the Canaanites and the Perizzites were living in the land.
Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no quarreling between you and me, or between your herdsmen and mine, for we are kinsmen, brothers.

versions.text: Abram said to Lot, "Let there be no quarreling between you and me, or between your herdsmen and mine, for we are family.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom 'men, brothers' stresses close kinship and echoes 'each from his brother' in v. 11; 'family' is vaguer and loses the verbal link within the chapter.

text: Isn't the whole land before you? Please separate from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left."

versions.text: Isn't the whole land before you? Let us part company. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew is a polite imperative addressed to Lot ('separate, please, from me'), inviting Lot to choose; the current rendering turns it into a mutual proposal and drops the courteous נָא.

text: Lot looked up and saw the whole Jordan Valley, that it was well watered everywhere—this was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah—like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt, all the way to Zoar.
So Lot chose the whole Jordan Valley for himself and set out eastward, and the two men parted from each other.
Abram settled in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled among the cities of the valley and pitched his tents as far as Sodom.
Now the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD.
After Lot had parted from him, the LORD said to Abram, "Look up and look around from where you stand—north and south, east and west.
All the land you see I will give to you and to your offspring forever.
I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth: if anyone could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted.
Rise up, walk through the land, its length and its breadth, for I am giving it to you."
So Abram moved his tents, and he came and settled by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.

versions.text: So Abram moved on and settled by the oaks of Mamre at Hebron, and there he built an altar to the LORD.
versions.explanation: The verb וַיֶּאֱהַל means 'to move/pitch tents' (the same verb used of Lot in v. 12, where the translation keeps the tent imagery); 'moved on' loses that link and also omits the intervening verb 'came'.
